newsitem.title: CHINA: HK property cools, may stall anti-speculation move.
newsitem.headline: HK property cools, may stall anti-speculation move.

text.p: The Hong Kong government's well-publicised concern about high property prices has taken some of the speculative edge out of the property market and may prevent official action against speculators, analysts said on Thursday.
The government has vowed to increase housing supply to bring prices to affordable levels but chief executive Tung Chee-hwa has said he may also slap punitive measures on speculators.
Analysts expect more details in a government statement in October.
"The government is huffing and puffing and the market has started to cool down already," said James Osborn, sales director at ING Barings.

Analysts said prices had slipped about five percent at some residential estates since Tung announced his housing plans in his inaugural speech on July 1 when China resumed control of the former British territory.
Merrill Lynch predicted in a recent report a 10-15 percent fall in residential property prices in the third quarter.
Cheung Kong (Holdings) Ltd offered flats last week at its Vista Paradiso project in the New Territories at prices below market expectations, influencing price movements in the market, analysts said.

The sale of only 80 percent of the units offered at Sun Hung Kai Properties Ltd's Grand Del Sol project in the New Territories on the first sale day last Saturday also pointed to reduced speculative activity, analysts added.
"People are listening to the government and the speculative activity seems to have slowed down a bit," said Serena Lau, managing director at Francis Lau & Co (Surveyors) Ltd.
Colliers Jardine said the number of residential property transactions eased to 17,300 in June from 19,550 in May.
"July seems to be a bit quieter than June," a researcher at the real estate group said.
Analysts said the government would focus on supply measures and avoid moves which could have far-reaching implications for Hong Kong and the health of its property market.
"A capital gains tax would not only influence the property market, but our banking system, the whole taxation system. The result would be too great," said Lau.
Peter Churchouse, managing director at Morgan Stanley Asia, said the government would be delighted if the market traded sideways. "They don't want to see it crash," he said.
"Supply side measures will go ahead whatever happens but the demand side measures are likely to be moderated if the market cools down," he said.
Tung has said he would like to boost housing supply to a target of at least 85,000 units a year.

Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Wednesday the government expected housing supply at about 79,000 units each year over the next three years and about 104,000 units a year in the following five years.
However, Edward Chan, head of research at Amsteel Securities, said housing supply would still fall short of demand and the government's warnings may only curb speculation in the near term.
"If speculators see that there will continue to be a slight imbalance between supply and demand, they will come back in the medium term," he said.
Michael Leary, senior property analyst at Lehman Brothers, said the government had not really addressed how it would increase supply.
"There has been a decline in transaction activity and asking prices are being adjusted downwards," he said. "But I think that the jury is going to be out on this for the time being."
